about: Lesson F10's own inputs: seven real energy balances (the United States, the European Union, China, India, Japan, Brazil and Norway), each as its national statistics publisher or the EU's statistics office published it, one data year per country, with the rows used, the units and the conversions; the accounting conventions; the four lenses; the regional card each country opens; the numbers to remember. Every value here was read on the cited page or table between 2 and 7 November 2026. Prairieland's numbers are read from prairieland.json at run time, never copied here.
subEffNotes: The rule: each MWh from nuclear, hydro, wind and solar counts as the fuel a thermal plant would burn to make it.
The assumption: publishers have used different plant efficiencies in different years; this page uses one round value, 40%, for every real country.
The exception: Prairieland uses its own fleet's efficiency, read from its file.

mtep.label: million t of oil equivalent (Mtep; Brazil's tep is 10⁷ kcal)

wso.label: Wind, solar and other power
wso.say: wind, solar and other renewable electricity
wso.note: Wind, solar and other renewable electricity, with bio-power and small hydro

hws.label: Hydro, wind and solar power
hws.note: Hydro, wind and solar electricity, after net exports

bio.label: Bioenergy
bio.note: Biofuels, wood and the renewable part of waste, as each publisher counts them

geoheat.label: Geothermal, ambient heat and tide
geoheat.note: Geothermal heat, the outdoor heat that heat pumps take in, and tide

recov.label: Waste and recovered heat (not split)
recov.note: Waste burned for energy, and heat and power recovered in industry, which the publisher counts as a source and does not split into renewable and fossil parts

waste.label: Waste (renewable part not split)
waste.note: Waste the publisher does not split into renewable and non-renewable parts

countries.name: United States
countries.otherNote: electricity and coal coke net imports, and rounding
countries.finalNote: U.S. final energy is EIA's end-use energy, which keeps some of the energy industry's own use: natural gas lease and plant fuel in industry, pipeline fuel in transport.

prov.method: Nuclear at its plants' average heat rate; hydro, wind, solar and geothermal electricity at 3,412 Btu per kWh since September 2023, close to physical energy content.
prov.coverage: Final energy is EIA's end-use energy (Tables 2.2 to 2.5); it keeps gas lease and plant fuel in industry and pipeline fuel in transport (Table 4.3). Farms sit inside industry.
prov.adjust: Non-fuel use (6.5 quads) shown apart as non-energy use; geothermal (0.117 quads) drawn as its own source; solar includes small-scale solar (Table 10.6).

countries.resources: Crude oil, natural gas and coal.
countries.institutions: Seven [[rto|independent grid operators]] (ISOs and RTOs) run wholesale markets; elsewhere [[vertically-integrated-utility|vertically integrated utilities]] own plants and wires. Three main grids, weakly linked.

countries.name: European Union (27 countries)
countries.otherNote: non-renewable waste and electricity and heat trade

prov.method: Physical energy content: nuclear as reactor heat; hydro, wind and solar photovoltaic as their gross electricity (nrg_bal_peh).
prov.coverage: Includes 1,704 PJ of fuel for international shipping, shown apart. Bioenergy is renewables less the other renewable sources, so it holds the renewable part of waste; non-renewable waste sits in 'other'.
prov.adjust: Coal includes peat and oil shale; solar includes solar heat (164 PJ); geothermal, ambient heat and tide drawn as one source.

importDep.text: Eurostat's import dependency rate: net imports ÷ gross available energy

production.split: renewables 48.1%, nuclear heat 28.2%, oil 3.3% and natural gas 5.1% of that production

countries.institutions: Separate companies make, carry and sell power ([[unbundling|unbundled]]). Each [[bidding-zone|price zone]] has its own price; [[market-coupling|coupled markets]] link the zones a day ahead and within the day.

countries.name: China

prov.published: 571,327 × 10,000 t of coal equivalent (5.71 billion t, about 167 EJ): coal 54.8%, oil 18.8%, gas 8.5%, primary electricity and other energy 17.9%.
prov.method: Coal equivalent: nuclear, hydro, wind and solar electricity counted at the coal burned per kWh in the year's thermal plants, a kind of substitution.
prov.coverage: Partial: the 'other energy' inside NBS's 17.9% is not split by NBS and is left out. Final energy is not drawn.
prov.adjust: Physical content is the page's estimate: fossil fuels as published, plus the four sources' TWh (nuclear ÷ 0.33). Solar from the 2023 Communiqué; the rest from the 2025 Yearbook.

countries.noFinal: China's statistics count the electricity users buy at the coal burned to make it; this page has not converted its final energy to the others' basis, so it shows China's primary energy only.
countries.coverage: partial estimate: NBS's 'other energy' left out

importDep.text: net imports ÷ total energy consumption, both in coal equivalent

countries.institutions: State-owned grid companies; each province largely decides which of its own plants run; markets that trade power for the next day and hour are moving toward one national market.

countries.name: India
countries.coverage: traditional biomass is not in the balance

prov.published: 903,158 ktoe (37,813 PJ) of total primary energy supply.
prov.method: Hydro, wind and solar at their electricity (1 GWh = 0.086 ktoe); nuclear at its electricity ÷ 0.33.
prov.coverage: No row for firewood or other traditional biomass: every share here is of the sources the balance covers.
prov.adjust: Coal includes lignite; oil is crude oil less net exports of products. Wind, solar and other renewable power includes bio-power and small hydro. 'Other' final use is farms and non-specified uses.

countries.institutions: State distribution companies (DISCOMs) buy most power under long-term contracts; one national grid running at one frequency ([[synchronous-grid|synchronous]]).

countries.name: Japan

pubElec.note: METI counts each kWh from these sources at the table's 8.4884 MJ (its primary-side factor; 3.6 MJ on the consumption side): a substitution. Solar's kWh are its photovoltaic power; its 4,996 TJ of solar heat stay as published.

countries.coverage: converted from METI's counting of electricity; fuels at [[gross-calorific-value|gross calorific value]]; waste and recovered heat counted

prov.published: 17,461,344 TJ (17.5 EJ) of domestic primary energy supply, fiscal year 2024, final figures.
prov.method: Fuels at their gross calorific value. Nuclear, hydro, solar, wind and geothermal electricity at 8.49 MJ per kWh, the fuel of a thermal plant at 42.4%: a kind of substitution.
prov.coverage: Waste burned for energy, and heat and power recovered in industry (573,930 TJ), count as a source: the page keeps them, as neither renewable nor fossil.
prov.adjust: Physical content is the page's conversion: each kWh at 3.6 MJ, nuclear's and geothermal's as heat (÷ 0.33, ÷ 0.10). Coal includes coal products; farms and fishing sit in industry.

importDep.text: net imports ÷ domestic primary energy supply, both as METI publishes them

production.split: electricity from nuclear and renewables counted at METI's 8.49 MJ per kWh

countries.resources: Little coal, oil or gas of its own.
countries.institutions: Ten utility areas, nine of them linked; the east runs at 50 Hz and the west at 60 Hz ([[frequency|grid frequency]]), joined by small converter links. Customers choose their supplier; there is a power exchange (JEPX) and a [[capacity-market|capacity market]].

countries.name: Brazil

prov.published: 328.5 Mtep of domestic energy supply (Oferta Interna de Energia).
prov.method: Hydro, wind and solar at their electricity (1 kWh = 860 kcal); nuclear at its electricity ÷ 0.33.
prov.coverage: Bioenergy: sugarcane products 52.0, firewood and charcoal 27.1, black liquor and other renewables 29.2 Mtep. Hydro includes imported electricity; solar includes solar heat.
prov.adjust: The energy sector's own use, inside BEN's final consumption, moved before the meter, as the others count it. Services, farms and the energy sector split by their published shares.

countries.institutions: One national grid, mostly hydro; plants run in order of their modelled costs; power is bought at auctions or traded in a free market.

countries.name: Norway
countries.coverage: its electricity, net of trade, counted as renewable: hydro, wind and solar made 98.7% of 2025's generation

prov.published: 326 TWh of net domestic energy supply (Table 2; its rows add to 326.2).
prov.method: Electricity at its own energy content (1 MWh = 3.6 GJ): production less net exports, not split by source (hydro made 89.9% of 2025's generation).
prov.coverage: Waste (5.2 TWh) is not split into renewable and non-renewable parts: the page counts it as neither.
prov.adjust: Buildings are households only: services sit in 'other' with farms and fishing.

importDep.text: net imports ÷ net domestic energy supply

countries.resources: Oil and gas, mostly for export; rivers for its own electricity.
countries.institutions: Nord Pool's [[bidding-zone|price zones]]; since October 2024 [[flow-based-coupling|flow-based coupling]] limits trades by the flow on each line; hydro, and dense [[hvdc|HVDC]] links.

prairieland.name: Prairieland
prairieland.institutions: Fictional: the course does not set out its institutions.

conventions.label: Physical energy content
conventions.who: the IEA, Eurostat and five of the seven publishers on this page (not China's or Japan's)
conventions.text: Nuclear counts as its reactors' heat (measured, or electricity ÷ 0.33 if unknown); hydro, wind and solar as the electricity they make.

conventions.label: Substitution
conventions.who: the Energy Institute's former method; China's coal equivalent and Japan's balance are kinds of it
conventions.text: Every MWh from nuclear, hydro, wind and solar counts as the fuel a thermal plant would burn to make it.

conventions.label: Direct equivalent
conventions.text: Every MWh from nuclear, hydro, wind and solar counts at its electricity, 3.6 GJ.
conventions.note: A lower bound: no conversion losses counted for any of them.

lenses.label: Import dependence
lenses.text: net imports as a share of primary energy: high for countries with few fuels of their own.

lenses.label: Resources
lenses.text: what the country produces at home: rivers, coal, oil, gas, crops.

lenses.label: Climate
lenses.text: buildings' share of final energy: heating and cooling raise it, and so do bigger homes, higher incomes and how statistics group services; the table cannot tell these apart.

lenses.label: Institutions
lenses.text: who runs the power system and how electricity is traded, from the regional cards.
